heading: Soil health and composting
body: Soil is more than the ground under your feet.
It is a living place. It feeds the crops, keeps water, and carries your harvest too.
In this module, learn to understand the soil, make safe compost, protect bare soil, and use cover crops and worm farms.

heading: Why it matters
body: The condition of the soil affects the roots, the water and the harvest.
Repeated bare soil, compaction and the loss of organic matter can damage it. Colour alone does not describe the whole condition.
Look at your soil, then choose ways of protecting and improving it.

heading: Learning outcomes
body: Look for many signs of soil condition.
Use a jar to investigate the soil's texture, knowing its limits.
Look after a compost heap, protect bare soil, and separate worm castings from the liquid that drips out.

heading: Soil is alive
body: Soil contains many kinds of living things. Bacteria and fungi help in the rotting of organic matter and circulate nutrients.
Some fungi help roots to obtain nutrients. Worm tunnels can help water and air to enter the soil.
Look at the roots, the soil structure and the movement of water, together with the visible life of the soil.

heading: Look: read your soil
body: Look carefully at these two soil examples.
First, look at the soil structure. In the field, observe how a moist lump breaks.
Look at the roots and the spaces around them.
Look at the covering on the surface. Loose mulch covers the other example.
Use many signs together. Colour alone cannot tell you about the health of the soil. Check moisture, plant growth and how water enters the soil.

heading: Investigate soil texture with a jar
body: Put soil and water in a clear jar, together with a little suitable detergent for separating soil particles (dispersing detergent). Close it and shake it, then leave it without being disturbed.
Sand begins to settle. Silt (soil finer than sand) follows, while clay can stay suspended in the water for a very long time.
This is a simple learning experiment. Lumps and clay that has not yet settled can mislead you; use a soil laboratory when you need accurate texture.

heading: Read the jar carefully
body: A solid layer of sand under cloudy water does not yet tell you the final proportion. Some fine particles may still be suspended in the water.
Compare the settled layers and test the soil by hand in the field.
Write down what you see and everything that is still uncertain. Do not decide on irrigation or a soil treatment based on one jar only.

heading: Investigate before treating
body: Soil compaction, poor drainage of water and the loss of organic matter can reduce roots and soil life.
A pale colour or few worms does not prove that chemicals have killed the soil. Worm activity changes with moisture and the season of the year.
Look at the patterns across the whole field. Check the management history, water draining away and plant growth before choosing a treatment.

heading: Compost that feeds the soil
body: Compost is organic matter that has rotted under controlled conditions.
Finished compost can improve soil structure and contributes to nutrients.
The time to ripeness varies by materials, moisture, air and heat. The name of a pound/province or a fixed number of weeks is not a test of readiness.

heading: Look: build a compost heap
body: Build a heap with dry brown materials (browns) and fresh green materials (greens).
Keep the layers moist, not watery, so that air and the decomposers (decomposers) can work.

heading: Balance browns and greens
body: Mix dry browns and fresh greens. Avoid dense, wet layers that shut out air.
If the heap becomes slippery or smells strongly of ammonia, add dry browns and turn it.
Check moisture and air as the heap changes; one recipe does not suit every mixture of materials.

heading: Heat alone is not a safety test
body: A medium warm degree does not confirm that every part of the heap has been treated. Time, heat and management are all important.
Do not put in meat, milk and dairy products, diseased plants, pet/domestic animal waste and contaminated things in this simple home process.
Do not think that making compost at home destroys all weed seed or all disease-causing living things. Use a monitored process where cleanliness is needed.

heading: Keep seed pods and contaminants out
body: Do not put wattle seed pods in the compost heap. An ordinary heap may not make every seed unable to grow.
Use only clean, untreated materials. Tree bark rots slowly; the word 'bark' alone does not confirm that it is not contaminated.
Check the heap and turn it when it needs air or more mixing. Keep it moist rather than full of water.

heading: Look: bare soil and mulch
body: Compare bare soil with covered soil.

When rain hits mulch instead of bare soil, much of the energy of the raindrops is dissipated. This picture only shows the idea of surface impact; it does not predict how water will move in a particular place.

heading: Mulch protects the soil
body: Cover bare soil with suitable, clean mulch, such as straw, dry grass or wood chips.
Mulch can reduce loss of water through evaporation, soften the beating of rain and prevent weeds.
Keep it away from the stems of trees and of crops. Check moisture underneath and adjust the layer; more mulch is not always better.

heading: Cover crops between seasons
body: Cover crops can protect the soil between the main crops. Choose according to local climate, available water and the following planting.
Examples of the course include oats, lupins, sunn hemp and cowpea. Check local suitability before sowing.
Legumes (plants like beans) need suitable bacteria and growing conditions in order to capture nitrogen. The nutrients left in them become available as the material rots.

heading: Worm castings and the liquid that drips out
body: Worm farms can turn suitable food scraps and bedding into worm castings. Check the box rather than waiting for a fixed harvest date.
The liquid that naturally drips in a worm box is called leachate. It is not the same thing as tea of prepared worm castings.
Leachate may contain dangerous living things or dangerous substances. Do not use it on edible crops or think that diluting it with water makes it safe.

heading: Protect the soil all year
body: A Highveld field left bare after the maize harvest faces two main dangers.
Winter wind can carry away dry topsoil.
The first big storm of spring can beat bare soil and damage its surface and structure. If water runs across the field, it can carry away loose soil.
Cover crops, mulch and organic matter can help to hold the soil in place and keep it alive.

heading: Field work
body: Check the soil in the place where you work. Record colour, structure, roots, moisture and any worm tracks (tunnels).
Compare with another place and note recent weather and management.
Try the jar experiment. Write down what it suggests, what is uncertain, and whether a lab test or a local adviser could help.

heading: Field action
body: Start one soil-building action from this module.
Cover bare soil with mulch, start a balanced compost heap, sow a suitable cover crop, or prepare a worm farm.
If your compost smells of ammonia and is slippery, add dry carbon such as straw and turn it.
Build soil life step by step.
